screens.title: Introduction to Solana Programs and Anchor
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll frame why Solana programs look different from smart contracts you may have seen elsewhere. On Solana, programs are deployed pieces of executable code that do not themselves hold application state. Instead, they operate on separate accounts that contain data. That separation is central to Solana’s performance model, and it changes how you design program logic and user flows. We will also explain why Rust is the common language for writing these programs: it gives you systems-level performance and memory safety that matter when programs manipulate account data and run in a concurrent runtime. Finally, we introduce the Anchor framework, which provides a domain-specific approach to defining instructions, accounts, and errors so you can avoid repeating low-level parsing and validation. A practical orientation follows: you will learn how to install Rust, the Solana CLI, and the Anchor CLI, initialize an Anchor project, and inspect the program and test folders. By the end, you should understand the separation of code and data, know why Rust is chosen, and appreciate how Anchor streamlines safety and developer productivity. Consider: how does separating code from data change the way you think about state updates in a blockchain program?

screens.title: What is a Solana Program?
screens.narratorSegment: A Solana program is executable code deployed to the network that defines application logic but does not hold state itself. Instead, programs operate on data contained in accounts that are passed into an instruction. When a transaction invokes a program, the runtime supplies the program with a set of accounts and instruction data; the program reads and writes account data and then returns. This separation means you must explicitly design how account data is structured, who owns accounts, and which accounts a program expects. A concrete example is a counter program: the program contains the increment logic, while the counter value lives in an account that the program updates. A common misconception is to think programs persist variables internally between calls. On Solana, persistent values live in accounts, so every state update modifies account data, not the program binary. That design supports high throughput and parallel execution because the runtime can schedule programs independently of where data lives. Takeaway: treat programs as pure logic and accounts as the persistent storage you design and validate. How will you map your application’s state into accounts for safe updates?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Programs are stateless executables; accounts carry persistent state and must be provided to instructions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a Solana Program?
Definition

Program as executable logic

Programs implement business rules but do not store persistent variables. Persisted data lives in accounts handed to the program at call time.

Example: Counter
The counter program holds increment logic. The counter value itself is stored in a separate account that the program updates when invoked.
Common misconception
Programs do not keep in-memory state between transactions. Always design persistent state as accounts.
Key Takeaway

Think of programs as pure functions and accounts as the file or database where you persist values.

Annotated flow
When a transaction calls a program, it supplies:
  • Instruction data that tells the program what operation to perform.
  • A set of accounts the program may read or write.
  • Signer and rent-exemption context for security and fees.
Analogy
Imagine a function in a library: the function code is fixed and stateless; you pass it files or records to operate on. Accounts are those files.

screens.title: Program Invocation and Program ID
screens.narratorSegment: Every deployed program on Solana is identified by a Program ID, a public key that acts as the address for that executable. When you build and deploy a program, you register a Program ID so transactions can route instructions to that program. Invocation means a transaction includes an instruction that names the Program ID and provides the accounts and instruction data the program will use. A simple concrete example: to call a token transfer program you include the token program’s Program ID and accounts representing source, destination, and authority. A misconception is thinking Program IDs change automatically; they are stable until you deploy a new program at a different address. Program ownership and correct account assignment are essential: the runtime enforces which programs may write to which accounts. For development, Anchor. toml and your deployment scripts record Program IDs; tests use those IDs to invoke the right code. Closing question: when you design your application, which accounts will you require to be signers and which will be writable, and how will the Program ID enforce access? Program Invocation and Program ID means a program id is the stable public key that identifies deployed program logic and routes invocations to it.. In practical terms, how programs are identified and called on solana. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Program Invocation
Architecture

Program ID and invocation

The runtime routes instructions to a program using its Program ID. The transaction includes accounts and data the program will act on.

Program ID
An immutable public key that identifies deployed executable logic.
Accounts
Passed into instructions as the source of persistent state.
Instruction Data
Parameters that tell the program which operation to perform.
Concrete scenario
Token transfer call
You include the token program’s Program ID, the source and destination accounts, and the authority signer. The program enforces permissions and updates account balances.
Key Takeaway

Program IDs route calls; correct account and signer designation are required for safe updates.

screens.title: Why Rust for Solana Programs?
screens.narratorSegment: Rust is the primary language for writing Solana programs because it provides systems-level performance together with strong compile-time memory safety guarantees. Performance matters because programs execute inside a runtime that expects efficiency and low overhead when accessing and mutating account data. Memory safety helps prevent common vulnerabilities like out-of-bounds reads or use-after-free errors that could corrupt account state or open attack surfaces. A concrete example is handling serialized data structures stored in accounts: Rust’s strict typing and ownership model reduce runtime surprises and make reasoning about lifetimes explicit. A typical misconception is that any language with good libraries is equally safe; while higher-level languages may ease developer ergonomics, they often rely on runtime behavior that is harder to audit for low-level memory issues. In Solana, where correctness and predictable execution costs matter, Rust’s combination of performance and safety is why it is the practical choice. Takeaway: learning Rust provides both the mental model and tooling to write correct programs that interact with account data safely. Why Rust for Solana Programs? means rust delivers performance and compile-time safety that align with solana’s low-level account and runtime requirements.. In practical terms, performance, memory safety, and predictable control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Why Rust
Definition

Rust for systems safety and speed

Rust’s ownership and type system reduce common memory errors and make low-level code easier to audit. Its performance profile aligns with Solana’s runtime constraints.

Concrete: serialized account data
When you parse and mutate serialized data in accounts, Rust’s explicit lifetimes and types make it safer and auditable compared with ad hoc parsing strategies.
Misconception
Safety isn’t automatic in other languages; runtime behavior can hide bugs that surface as security issues on-chain.
Why it matters

Choosing Rust isn’t just about language preference. It shapes how you design serialization, error handling, and concurrency. When writing programs that mutate shared account state, predictable behavior matters for audits and correctness.

Key Takeaway

Rust’s safety and performance directly support secure, auditable Solana program development.

screens.title: Raw Solana Development vs Anchor
screens.narratorSegment: Developing directly against the Solana Program Library and raw Rust forces you to handle account validation, serialization, and instruction parsing manually. That gives you maximum control but increases boilerplate and the surface area for mistakes. Anchor provides a domain-specific framework that abstracts many repetitive tasks: it supplies macros and a DSL to declare instruction interfaces, account structures, and custom error types. This automation reduces the amount of code you write and standardizes validation, which improves auditability and developer productivity. A concrete example is account validation: instead of writing many lines to check ownership and signer flags every time, Anchor lets you declare constraints and enforces them automatically. A common misconception is that frameworks remove the need to understand underlying mechanics. Anchor does not replace the need to know how accounts work; rather, it moves repetitive, error-prone work into well-tested patterns. Takeaway: use Anchor to accelerate development while retaining responsibility for high-level design and account layout decisions. How might Anchor’s abstractions change how you write tests for your program? Raw Solana Development vs Anchor means anchor abstracts validation and parsing, reducing boilerplate while you still design account layout and logic.. In practical terms, where anchor reduces boilerplate and risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Raw vs Anchor
Raw Solana
You write manual parsers, account checks, and error handling. This is flexible but verbose and error-prone.
Risk
More boilerplate increases opportunities for mistakes in validation and parsing.
Anchor
Anchor gives macros and a DSL for declaring instructions and accounts, automating common validation and reducing repetition.
Benefit
Fewer lines of code and standardized patterns improve auditability and developer speed.
Example
Anchor lets you declare constraints for an account and enforces them, avoiding repetitive checks.
Misconception
Anchor doesn’t remove the need to understand accounts; you must still design the layout correctly.
Key Takeaway

Use Anchor to reduce boilerplate but continue to reason about account design and security.

screens.title: Install Rust, Solana CLI, and Anchor CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Before you write or build programs, install and verify the core tools. First, ensure rustup is installed; it provides Rust and Cargo, the package manager. Next, install the Solana CLI so you can manage keys, configure a cluster, and deploy programs. Finally, install the Anchor CLI to build, test, and manage Anchor projects. For each step, you will run the installer once and then confirm successful installation by checking the version output. If your shell reports a command not found, the most common fix is that the tool’s installation directory is not on your PATH; restarting the terminal or manually adding the directory fixes that. A safety point: always run installers from the official source and review scripts before executing them to avoid supply-chain risks. Concrete example: after installing, run the version checks and expect readable output confirming the tool is present. Misconception: successful install messages in a script do not always mean the tool is accessible to your shell session. Restart and verify. Are your version checks returning expected outputs? In practical terms, verify your toolchain before initializing a project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Install Toolchain
Installers
Use the language installer for Rust, the Solana CLI installer, and the Anchor CLI installer. After running each installer, check versions to confirm success.
Example command output checks
rustc --version
solana --version
anchor --version
Troubleshoot

If a command returns "not found," restart your terminal or add the installer bin path to your PATH environment variable.

Notes
  • Prefer the official installers provided by the tool maintainers.
  • Use the locked and force flags when installing Anchor CLI to ensure a consistent build.
  • Verify with version commands and inspect the shell PATH if necessary.
Key Takeaway

Installers set up tools but verification is essential to confirm a working environment before creating a project.

The exact installer commands are shown below in the reference panel for you to copy into a terminal. Review them before running.
Reference installer commands
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
sh -c "$(curl -sSfL https://release.solana.com/v1.18.4/install)"
cargo install --git https://github.com/coral-xyz/anchor anchor-cli --locked --force

screens.title: Initialize and Inspect an Anchor Project
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing an Anchor project scaffolds a workspace with folders you will use every day. Run the init command to create a directory that contains programs, tests, and a configuration file. The programs directory holds the Rust program code you will build and deploy. Tests contains TypeScript or JavaScript tests that run against a local validator or test environment to exercise your program’s behavior. Anchor. toml is the central configuration file where workspace members and Program IDs are declared; it is used by Anchor’s build and deployment tooling. A concrete example: after running anchor init my-counter-app you should see a programs folder containing a Rust crate for your counter program and a tests folder with a starter test that deploys the program to a local validator and runs assertions. A common mistake is to expect the scaffold to include everything for production; instead, treat it as a starting point. Takeaway: use the scaffold to focus on program logic, but inspect Anchor. toml and tests to ensure deployment settings and Program IDs match your environment. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Anchor Init
Scaffold

anchor init my-counter-app

The command scaffolds a workspace. Key folders are programs/, tests/, and the Anchor.toml configuration file.

Directory layout
my-counter-app/
├─ programs/
│  └─ my_counter_program/
│     └─ src/lib.rs
├─ tests/
│  └─ my_counter_test.ts
└─ Anchor.toml
Inspect
Open Anchor.toml to confirm workspace members and program IDs. Update IDs for your deployment targets as needed.
Key Takeaway

Use the generated structure as a starting point: programs contain Rust code and tests validate behavior against a local validator.

screens.title: Anchor.toml and Project Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor. toml is the configuration file Anchor uses to record workspace members, program IDs, and test settings. When you initialize a project, Anchor. toml defines which programs belong to the workspace and what Program IDs are associated with each. During development you will update this file when you deploy programs to new addresses or when you share the project with collaborators who use different local deploy targets. A concrete example: you may replace the placeholder Program ID with the address produced by your build and deploy step so tests point to the correct program. A frequent mistake is leaving the scaffolded Program ID unchanged when running tests against a real validator, causing tests to invoke the wrong address. The Anchor. toml structure helps centralize configuration so builds and tests use consistent settings. Takeaway: inspect and update Anchor. toml as part of your deployment workflow to ensure tests and deployments target the expected Program IDs. In practical terms, where program ids and workspace settings live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Anchor.toml
Config file

Anchor.toml

This file records workspace members and program IDs. Use it to align builds, deployments, and tests.

Example snippet
[programs.localnet]
my_counter_program = "ReplaceWithProgramID"

[workspace]
members = ["programs/*"]
Practical notes
  • Update Program IDs after deploy.
  • Ensure tests point to the same config environment.
  • Share and document environment differences with collaborators.
Key Takeaway

Anchor.toml keeps your workspace aligned; treat it as the source of truth for program addresses used in tests and deploys.

screens.title: Common Setup Mistakes and Safety Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When setting up your environment, a few recurring issues appear. The most common is the PATH not including the newly installed executables, which leads to the shell reporting commands as not found. The usual remedies are restarting the terminal or adding the installer’s bin directory to your PATH environment variable. Another point is installer flags: when installing Anchor CLI the chapter recommends using locked and force flags to ensure a consistent, up-to-date build; this helps avoid version mismatches. Verification is essential: run version commands for rustc, solana, and anchor, and interpret their outputs to confirm the final state. For safety, always inspect installer scripts and prefer official release commands rather than third-party mirrors to reduce supply-chain risk. A concrete example: after installing, run the version checks and confirm the versions are present; if not, investigate PATH and retry. Takeaway: install carefully, verify outputs, and treat configuration as the likely source of initial errors when a tool appears missing. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, Solana programs are stateless executables that act on data provided in accounts; account design is central to correct behavior. Second, Rust is the practical language for writing Solana programs because it provides performance and compile-time memory safety that reduce low-level errors when parsing and mutating account data. Third, Anchor is a framework that simplifies common patterns such as account validation, deserialization, and error handling by offering a DSL and macros. These three concepts—stateless programs with accounts, Rust’s role, and Anchor’s abstractions—form the foundation for building Solana programs effectively. As you move into hands-on work, keep these ideas in mind and review the scaffolded project structure to confirm Program IDs and tests align with your environment. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll frame why Solana programs look different from smart contracts you may have seen elsewhere. On Solana, programs are deployed pieces of executable code that do not themselves hold application state. Instead, they operate on separate accounts that contain data. That separation is central to Solana’s performance model, and it changes how you design program logic and user flows. We will also explain why Rust is the common language for writing these programs: it gives you systems-level performance and memory safety that matter when programs manipulate account data and run in a concurrent runtime. Finally, we introduce the Anchor framework, which provides a domain-specific approach to defining instructions, accounts, and errors so you can avoid repeating low-level parsing and validation. A practical orientation follows: you will learn how to install Rust, the Solana CLI, and the Anchor CLI, initialize an Anchor project, and inspect the program and test folders. By the end, you should understand the separation of code and data, know why Rust is chosen, and appreciate how Anchor streamlines safety and developer productivity. Consider: how does separating code from data change the way you think about state updates in a blockchain program?

These learning objectives guide our work. First, you will explain the fundamental role of programs on Solana: why they are stateless executables and how account data is provided to instructions. You will practice describing Program IDs and how programs are invoked. Second, you will understand why Rust is the primary language for Solana program development. This includes being able to describe Rust’s strengths for systems code and why those strengths matter when handling account memory and concurrency. Third, you will articulate the benefits of the Anchor framework: how it offers a domain-specific language, automates account validation, and reduces low-level parsing and error handling. Finally, you will set up a complete Solana development environment and initialize an Anchor project. That means successfully installing Rust, the Solana CLI, and Anchor CLI, verifying versions, and exploring the generated project structure including programs, tests, and Anchor. toml. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you can verify you completed the task with confidence.

This second objectives slide focuses on two practical outcomes. First, you will initialize a new Anchor project and navigate its directory structure so you can find where programs and tests live. The workspace created by anchor init includes a programs directory for Rust code and a tests folder for TypeScript or JavaScript tests that exercise your deployed program. You will learn to open Anchor. toml and identify workspace, program IDs, and test settings. Second, you will verify your toolchain and the common troubleshooting steps. For example, if the shell reports a command not found after installing a CLI, the most common solution is updating your PATH or restarting the terminal. You should be able to run version checks and interpret the output to confirm tools are correctly installed. These objectives prepare you for the hands-on activity where you install tools, initialize my-counter-app, and inspect program code and tests. Knowing where each piece lives helps you iterate quickly and avoid common mistakes during deployment.

A Solana program is executable code deployed to the network that defines application logic but does not hold state itself. Instead, programs operate on data contained in accounts that are passed into an instruction. When a transaction invokes a program, the runtime supplies the program with a set of accounts and instruction data; the program reads and writes account data and then returns. This separation means you must explicitly design how account data is structured, who owns accounts, and which accounts a program expects. A concrete example is a counter program: the program contains the increment logic, while the counter value lives in an account that the program updates. A common misconception is to think programs persist variables internally between calls. On Solana, persistent values live in accounts, so every state update modifies account data, not the program binary. That design supports high throughput and parallel execution because the runtime can schedule programs independently of where data lives. Takeaway: treat programs as pure logic and accounts as the persistent storage you design and validate. How will you map your application’s state into accounts for safe updates?

Every deployed program on Solana is identified by a Program ID, a public key that acts as the address for that executable. When you build and deploy a program, you register a Program ID so transactions can route instructions to that program. Invocation means a transaction includes an instruction that names the Program ID and provides the accounts and instruction data the program will use. A simple concrete example: to call a token transfer program you include the token program’s Program ID and accounts representing source, destination, and authority. A misconception is thinking Program IDs change automatically; they are stable until you deploy a new program at a different address. Program ownership and correct account assignment are essential: the runtime enforces which programs may write to which accounts. For development, Anchor. toml and your deployment scripts record Program IDs; tests use those IDs to invoke the right code. Closing question: when you design your application, which accounts will you require to be signers and which will be writable, and how will the Program ID enforce access? Program Invocation and Program ID means a program id is the stable public key that identifies deployed program logic and routes invocations to it.. In practical terms, how programs are identified and called on solana. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rust is the primary language for writing Solana programs because it provides systems-level performance together with strong compile-time memory safety guarantees. Performance matters because programs execute inside a runtime that expects efficiency and low overhead when accessing and mutating account data. Memory safety helps prevent common vulnerabilities like out-of-bounds reads or use-after-free errors that could corrupt account state or open attack surfaces. A concrete example is handling serialized data structures stored in accounts: Rust’s strict typing and ownership model reduce runtime surprises and make reasoning about lifetimes explicit. A typical misconception is that any language with good libraries is equally safe; while higher-level languages may ease developer ergonomics, they often rely on runtime behavior that is harder to audit for low-level memory issues. In Solana, where correctness and predictable execution costs matter, Rust’s combination of performance and safety is why it is the practical choice. Takeaway: learning Rust provides both the mental model and tooling to write correct programs that interact with account data safely. Why Rust for Solana Programs? means rust delivers performance and compile-time safety that align with solana’s low-level account and runtime requirements.. In practical terms, performance, memory safety, and predictable control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Developing directly against the Solana Program Library and raw Rust forces you to handle account validation, serialization, and instruction parsing manually. That gives you maximum control but increases boilerplate and the surface area for mistakes. Anchor provides a domain-specific framework that abstracts many repetitive tasks: it supplies macros and a DSL to declare instruction interfaces, account structures, and custom error types. This automation reduces the amount of code you write and standardizes validation, which improves auditability and developer productivity. A concrete example is account validation: instead of writing many lines to check ownership and signer flags every time, Anchor lets you declare constraints and enforces them automatically. A common misconception is that frameworks remove the need to understand underlying mechanics. Anchor does not replace the need to know how accounts work; rather, it moves repetitive, error-prone work into well-tested patterns. Takeaway: use Anchor to accelerate development while retaining responsibility for high-level design and account layout decisions.
